overview.text:
The Rann of Kutch is a vast seasonal salt marsh on Gujarat's border with Pakistan, split into the Great and Little Rann. In the monsoon it lies under water; as the water recedes it dries into a crust of white salt that glitters at sunrise, sunset and above all on full-moon nights.

Most visitors come for the Great Rann's White Rann at Dhordo, 81 km from Bhuj, where Gujarat Tourism's Rann Utsav tent city runs from 1 November 2026 to 7 March 2027 this season, with folk music, crafts and food. Entry to the White Rann and Kalo Dungar, Kutch's highest point, is by permit, since both lie in the border area. The Little Rann's Wild Ass Sanctuary protects the last Indian wild asses, and Bhuj, Mandvi and the Harappan city of Dholavira make a longer trip.

best_time.text: Come between November and early March. Rann Utsav – The Tent City runs from 1 November 2026 to 7 March 2027 this season, and full-moon nights are the most popular, when the White Rann glows. In the monsoon the Rann lies under water; the white crust only returns once it dries. For the Little Rann's wild asses and migratory birds, November to February is best.

The Rann Utsav and Indian Wild Ass Sanctuary make the Great and Little Rann a two-part trip.

overview.text:
Pachmarhi is Madhya Pradesh's only hill station, at about 1,100 m in a valley of the Satpura range. Its name means 'five caves', after the legend that the Pandavas sheltered here; the British developed it after Captain James Forsyth came across the plateau in 1857, and it is still a quiet cantonment town kept small by building limits.

The town sits inside the Pachmarhi Biosphere Reserve, on UNESCO's list since 2009, and the Satpura Tiger Reserve. Days here go on waterfalls such as Bee Falls and Apsara Vihar, the Jata Shankar cave shrine, viewpoints like Priyadarshini Point and Dhoopgarh — at 1,352 m the state's highest point — and rock paintings up to 10,000 years old. October to March is clearest; the monsoon fills the falls.

overview.text:
Gwalior grew around its hilltop fort, which legend says the chieftain Suraj Sen built after the hermit Gwalipa cured him. Inside 10-metre walls stand the Man Mandir palace, the twin 11th-century Sas-Bahu temples, the 100-ft Teli ka Mandir, Gurudwara Data Bandi Chhor and, on Gopachal Parvat, rock-cut figures of the 24 Jain Tirthankaras; an evening light and sound show tells the story.

The Chaturbhuj Temple carries the world's first written zero, and the city is the birthplace of Tansen, whose tomb hosts the five-day Tansen Samaroh each December — one reason UNESCO named Gwalior a Creative City of Music. Below the fort are the Scindias' Jai Vilas Palace museum, the Gujari Mahal museum and Rani Lakshmi Bai's samadhi. Eat bedai and take home gajak.

Gajak, a sesame-and-jaggery sweet to take home.

items.title: What is Gwalior famous for?
items.body: The fort, with Man Mandir, Sas-Bahu, Teli ka Mandir and Gopachal Parvat.

items.title: When is the Tansen Samaroh?
items.body: Every December, for five days.

items.title: Is there a light and sound show?
items.body: Yes, an evening light and sound show at the fort.

items.title: What day trips are there?
items.body: Mitaoli (37 km), Padavali (35 km) and the Bateshwar temples.
Seeing only Man Mandir and missing Gopachal Parvat's Jain sculptures.
Leaving before the fort's light and sound show.
Missing the Tansen Samaroh if you are visiting in December.
